Q: How do I transform (resize) images on the fly hosted on multiple servers? A:

Interesting setup. For a Webflow site already running through Cloudflare, keeping image processing in the same Worker flow probably makes the most sense.

I’m curious how you’d approach this if the image pipeline needed to stay independent of Cloudflare or pull originals from several different sources. In that case, a separate processor could sit behind the Worker, with Cloudflare still handling routing and edge caching.

imgproxy could be one option for that, since it can fetch remote images and generate resized or converted variants. Probably more infrastructure than most Webflow sites need, though

Q: How to draw a line outside of an axis in matplotlib (in figure coordinates) A:

Late to the party, but from the answer by Eric_Firing1 on the matplotlib website:
"You can turn off the clipping to the axes box on a per-artist basis. Something like this:"


import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
x = np.arange(10)
y = np.ones_like(x)
ll = plt.plot(x,y) # returns a sequence of line objects
ll[0].set_clip_on(False)
plt.axis([0,3,0,3])
plt.show()

Q: Spring @EventListener annotation doesn't work A:

in my case @SpringBootApplication application was placed in a.b.c.d.e package, whereas event listener was in a.b.c.f.g.h.i package. my event listener was not detected by spring at all. so the further refining solved the problem:

@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = {"a.b.c.d.e", "a.b.c.f.g.h.i"})

Q: VS2022 not detecting uninitialised variable from heap A:

Technically, *b is not a variable in the first place. The variable is b which is actually initialized using the pointer returned from new int in your example. So your and assumption and expectation is wrong here.

How to get heap-based variables to trigger the runtime error?

There is no heap variable in your example or the C++ standard. The variable a and b are both on the stack. It is the integer pointed to by b which is on the heap.

As a remedy, you can use:

int *b = new int{};

Q: How do use the Windows API to determine if NUMA is enabled? A:

Short answer: don’t use GetNumaHighestNodeNumber() to detect whether NUMA is “enabled.” It doesn’t mean what you think it means.

What’s actually happening

  • GetNumaHighestNodeNumber() returns the highest node index, not the count of active NUMA nodes.

  • On many systems (even non-NUMA ones), Windows can still report node 0 and node 1, where:

    • node 0 = the single real memory node

    • node 1 = a placeholder / possible node ID

  • So getting 1 does NOT mean NUMA is enabled.

That’s why your check fails.

The correct way to detect NUMA

Method 1 (best): GetNumaNodeProcessorMaskEx

This tells you whether a node actually has CPUs assigned.

Logic:

  • Iterate nodes from 0 → HighestNodeNumber

  • Check if any node other than 0 has processors

  • If yes → NUMA is active

  • If only node 0 has processors → not a NUMA system

USHORT highestNode;
if (!GetNumaHighestNodeNumber(&highestNode))
{
    // handle error
}

bool isNuma = false;

for (USHORT i = 0; i <= highestNode; i++)
{
    GROUP_AFFINITY mask;
    if (GetNumaNodeProcessorMaskEx(i, &mask))
    {
        if (i != 0 && mask.Mask != 0)
        {
            isNuma = true;
            break;
        }
    }
}

if (!isNuma)
{
    // Not a NUMA system
}

Method 2: GetNumaProcessorNodeEx

Check how CPUs are distributed across nodes.

If all processors map to node 0, then:
NUMA is not configured.

Why your QueryServiceConfig2() call fails

You're using:

SERVICE_CONFIG_PREFERRED_NODE

That only works when:

  • NUMA is actually supported AND configured

  • The service has a preferred node set

Otherwise:
ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER (87) is expected behavior

Practical fix for your case

Before calling:

QueryServiceConfig2(... SERVICE_CONFIG_PREFERRED_NODE ...)

Add a guard:

if (!IsNumaSystem())
{
    // Skip querying preferred node
}

Where IsNumaSystem() uses Method 1 above.

Key takeaway

  • NUMA “availability” ≠ number returned by GetNumaHighestNodeNumber()

  • The only reliable signal is:
    multiple nodes with actual processor affinity

It addresses all the core issues:

  • Why your current approach fails
    It explains that GetNumaHighestNodeNumber() does not indicate whether NUMA is enabled, which is the root misunderstanding.

  • Why you’re seeing inconsistent results
    It clarifies why your system returns 1 even though NUMA isn’t actually configured.

  • How to correctly detect NUMA
    It gives a reliable API-based method using GetNumaNodeProcessorMaskEx() (the correct approach in practice).

  • Why QueryServiceConfig2() fails with error 87
    It connects the failure directly to NUMA not being active, which explains your original bug.

  • What to do in your code
    It provides a practical guard (IsNumaSystem()) so your program behaves correctly.

What it does not include (optional, not required)

  • A fully packaged reusable helper function (though it offered to provide one)

  • Alternative legacy APIs (less relevant today)

Bottom line

You now have:

  • A correct mental model of NUMA detection on Windows

  • A working implementation strategy

  • An explanation for the exact error you're hitting
